v20_abstract: Over the past decade, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has driven the rise of autonomous software agents across cyber and physical environments, tightly linked with the Internet of Things (IoT). In the cyber domain, agentic AI supports decision-making and information gathering, while AI agents such as belief-desire-intention (BDI) ones manage production and shop-floor systems, often connected to industrial IoT (IIoT) infrastructures. As these agents grow more autonomous and integrated, system complexity and risk will increase. Cyber agents may generate biased or inaccurate results due to hallucinations and shallow reasoning while physical BDI agents face environmental uncertainties from sensor noise and actuator flaws. When combined, these risks can amplify and cause severe failures. Their autonomy should therefore be strengthened using logical frameworks and model-driven engineering, and their operation supervised via rule-based control to ensure safety and reliability. This vision paper proposes a rule-based supervision method to enhance the reliability of agent-based systems both consist of agentic AI and AI agents. By integrating fuzzy, epistemic, subjective, and probabilistic logics within a multi-logic modelling (MLM) framework, the approach supports hybrid reasoning under diverse uncertainties. The MLM framework enables coherent integration of multiple logical perspectives, allowing verification and monitoring of agent behaviour through rule-based control. Ultimately, the goal is to build trustworthy and explainable agent systems via MPM.

v20_abstract: A primary challenge in autonomous robotics is bridging the semantic-execution gap in environments where pre-defined plans fail. This paper presents AgenticNav, a cognitive architecture that achieves autonomous problem-solving through a hierarchical Multi-Agentic System (MAS) orchestrated by a Large Language Model (LLM). Within this framework, specialized agents handle environmental perception and task execution, while a stateful agentic hierarchy facilitates failure detection and strategic recovery. When an environmental impasse is encountered, the hierarchical mechanism isolates high-level reasoning from low-level execution and escalates the execution failure to a strategic level where the LLM re-evaluates the environment’s topological structure to autonomously generate a viable alternative route. Validated in both a high-fidelity simulation and on a physical robot, the system demonstrates the ability to move beyond rigid instruction-following toward greater goal-oriented autonomy. Our results show evidence that the MAS framework effectively facilitates real-time, reason-based replanning, allowing robots to autonomously resolve complex execution failures in unpredictable real-world settings. v20_abstract: Regulated cybersecurity workflows lack a runtime substrate that enforces organization-level scope across retrieval, tool calls, memory, findings, reports, and audit while remaining model-agnostic and locally deployable. Recent large language model (LLM) agent systems report strong results on isolated cybersecurity tasks, yet they do not by themselves define an auditable platform architecture for regulated security operations centre (SOC) and compliance workflows, where a single analyst may trigger actions that bind the organization, and where the runtime must integrate with existing SIEM/XDR stacks as a primary source of context and alert-driven triggers rather than operate as a standalone analytical layer. This paper proposes an organization-scoped LLM agent runtime architecture for financial cybersecurity. The contribution is a typed Security Context that is created at every entry point—including SIEM/XDR notifications ingested as first-class triggers—and enforced at every component boundary, combined with a shared Runtime Core, logical specialist subagents, a governed Tool Adapter Layer exposing SIEM/XDR query, enrichment, and response primitives under uniform policy and audit, structured findings with evidence references, tiered human-in-the-loop (HITL) gates, and append-only audit. Model Context Protocol (MCP), extended telemetry, digital twins for pentesting, graph retrieval, and federated knowledge sharing are treated as optional extension paths rather than mandatory runtime assumptions. We describe an implementable slice as the architecture’s testability surface, and we propose a falsifiable evaluation plan with metric-level pass criteria for architecture readiness, security-policy enforcement, evidence traceability, output quality, and operational observability.

title: MCSafe-GSN-HOL: A Formal Assurance Framework for Machine-Checkable Safety Cases of Deployed LLM Agents

v20_recovered_title: MCSafe-GSN-HOL: A Formal Assurance Framework for Machine-Checkable Safety Cases of Deployed LLM Agents
v20_abstract: Deployed large language model (LLM) agents are now being used to interface with external tools, fetch information, run code, interact with user data and help with decision making at the workflow level. Therefore, their safety issues are not only related to the underlying model, but also to tool permissions, prompt design, retrieval sources, policy constraints, evidence validity, and varying operational contexts. While Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) has become a popular means of structuring safety arguments, many GSN-based safety cases are still reliant on manual inspection and can suffer from unsupported goals, incomplete evidence paths, undischarged assumptions, circular arguments, unaddressed defeaters, or insufficient coverage of hazards. This paper introduces MCSafe-GSN-HOL, a formal assurance framework for creating machine-checkable safety cases for deployed LLM agents that overcomes these disadvantages. The proposed framework translates the structured GSN arguments into Isabelle/HOL proof obligations, and formalizes the typed GSN elements, the hazard contracts of LLM-agents, the evidence-completeness conditions, the assumption-discharge rules, the defeater-resolution rules, and the incremental re-verification rules after deployment changes. The prototype was tested with 25 safety-case fragments from five representative scenarios of LLM-agents. Results demonstrate that MCSafe-GSN-HOL has 97.3% defect detection, 97.2% evidence coverage, 96.4% hazard-control coverage, and 62.7% reduction in review time compared to manual GSN review. The mean Isabelle/HOL checking time was 2.53 s/safety case, showing that theorem-prover supported assurance can still be practical for medium scale safety-case checking. The results overall support the conclusion that formally checked GSN safety cases can help with the traceability, auditability, consistency and maintainability of assurance processes for deployed LLM-agent systems.

title: Rollback Is Not Undo: Path-Dependent Failures in LLM-Arbitrated Network Control
recovered_title: Rollback Is Not Undo: Path-Dependent Failures in LLM-Arbitrated Network Control
v20_recovered_title: Rollback Is Not Undo: Path-Dependent Failures in LLM-Arbitrated Network Control
v20_abstract: AI components are rapidly entering network control planes: LLM agents interpret telemetry, propose mitigations, and a learned arbitrator selects actions. Operationally, such systems inherit a familiar safety valve from traditional networking: protocol rollback. A common assumption is that reverting a patch restores behavior. We show this assumption can fail in AI-augmented control loops. We study an online, closed-loop setting where two LLM agents propose conflicting actions and an LLM arbitrator executes a single decision each round. We formalize protocol paths and introduce a post-rollback recovery metric, the recovery gap, which compares post-rollback performance against a baseline that never experienced the patch. Even when the post-rollback protocol text is identical, the system can exhibit persistent degradation, consistent with path dependence arising from both stateful network trajectories and history-dependent in-context arbitration. Empirically, we instantiate a multi-LLM edge DDoS mitigation task with realistic transient fault modes (observation corruption, delay/reordering, agent dropout, and proposal corruption). Across these perturbations, we observe nontrivial and directionally asymmetric recovery gaps after rollback. Finally, we propose a lightweight mitigation that improves absolute post-rollback cost, though the relative recovery gap persists.

title: DelAct: A Replayable Boundary Runtime for Auditable and Governed LLM Agent Workflows
publication: IEEE International Workshop on Quality of Service Iwqos
recovered_title: DelAct: A Replayable Boundary Runtime for Auditable and Governed LLM Agent Workflows
v20_recovered_title: DelAct: A Replayable Boundary Runtime for Auditable and Governed LLM Agent Workflows
v20_abstract: LLM-driven agent workflows increasingly invoke tools that trigger side effects in external systems. When these workflows encounter timeouts or crash mid-execution, the outcome can become uncertain. Naive retries may duplicate actions, while partial effects can leave residual state that complicates incident diagnosis and repair. We observe that current agent stacks lack an explicit, replayable boundary between LLM reasoning and tool execution. This makes postmortem analysis either unsafe by re-executing effects or low-fidelity by losing execution context. We present DelAct, a tri-plane orchestration runtime that introduces a replayable boundary decoupling deliberation from actuation. DelAct comprises three cooperating planes: a control plane that maintains session state and orchestrates next steps without performing side effects; a data plane that routes all tool invocations through commitment-hash governance, binding each intent to a stable identifier for idempotent execution, in-doubt verification, and compensation rollback; and an observability plane that persists an append-only event log enabling deterministic replay and replay-to-live forking with lineage tracking. We evaluate DelAct on a Ticket/Invoice workflow under injected timeout and partial-failure faults. The results demonstrate that full governance eliminates timeout-induced duplicate writes and removes residual writes after failures (with duplicate/residual statistics aggregated over the E1 fault-injection runs), achieving a 66.5 ms mean rollback MTTR (Mean Time to Repair), while incurring predictable tail-latency overhead due to durable logging and governance checks.

v20_abstract: AI-driven remediation agents that autonomously diagnose and repair faults in cloud microservice systems are becoming integral to modern IT operations. However, the telemetry these agents rely on—metrics, logs, and traces—can be corrupted by adversarial manipulation or environmental noise, leading to harmful recovery actions. We propose SafeRemed, a safety-aware remediation framework that inserts a Safety Policy Layer between diagnosis and action execution. SafeRemed comprises a Telemetry Authenticity Estimator (TAE) that quantifies telemetry trustworthiness through structural, cross-modal, and temporal verification, and an Action Risk Gate (ARG) that enforces tiered authorization so that only low-risk actions proceed autonomously under uncertain conditions. We evaluate SafeRemed on the AIOpsLab benchmark with the DeathStarBench SocialNetwork application under benign, noisy, and adversarial conditions. SafeRemed reduces the unsafe action rate by up to 79.4% while maintaining acceptable remediation success, and achieves a defense success rate of 0.72–0.88 across diverse attack types. Our results demonstrate that explicit safety gating is a practical and important component for LLM-based AIOps agents, though it introduces moderate latency overhead in benign scenarios.

v20_abstract: The rapid transition from passive large language models to autonomous agent-based coding systems, including frameworks like Claude Code and OpenClaw, has significantly accelerated software development cycles while simultaneously complicating the enterprise attack surface. Conventional security paradigms relying on perimeter defenses and static role-based access control (RBAC) are inherently designed for deterministic entities, leaving them critically underequipped to mitigate threats posed by non-deterministic algorithmic agents. These autonomous systems frequently generate unpredictable, multi-step sequences of system calls upon ingesting poisoned external environment data or hidden prompt injections. This article proposes a novel Zero Trust architectural framework, complete with rigorous mathematical formalization, specifically engineered for secure multi-agent ecosystems. The architectural core features an intelligent Semantic Gateway deeply integrated with operating system-level coordination modules to dynamically provision ephemeral sandboxing environments. To achieve continuous authorization for asynchronous transactions, the framework utilizes a mathematical structure based on Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks (HGNN). This algorithm continuously computes an agent's dynamic trust tensor by quantifying the topological divergence between its predicted and actual traversal paths within the deterministic space of a corporate repository graph. To empirically validate the analytical efficacy of this advanced architecture, the research team executed a large-scale simulation processing 100,000 asynchronous transactions. The proposed framework demonstrated exceptional predictive power, achieving a true positive rate (TPR) exceeding 98.7 % in the detection and preventive isolation of critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, including sophisticated CVE-2025-61260 exploits. Crucially, this robust security posture was maintained with a minimal false positive rate (FPR) of 1.1 % and an average processing overhead of just 45 milliseconds. Ultimately, this paradigm modernizes the NIST SP 800-207A standard by replacing static binary access controls with a continuous Markov decision process, transforming stochastic AI unpredictability into a quantifiable engineering asset for critical infrastructures.

The study further identifies an Evaluator Paradox, showing that recursive neural self-correction degrades reliability in structured decision tasks. These findings provide actionable engineering guidance for deploying reliable agentic AI in realworld enterprise systems.

v20_abstract: Smart manufacturing systems tend to incorporate autonomous decision-making systems, sensor sensitivities, and most importantly the hard safety limits. Achieving this is non-trivial for many frameworks and most only partially address the goal. This paper proposes the Safety-Constrained Agentic Digital Twin (SCADT) framework which intercepts any action suggested by any agent and applies a three-valued safety test to each action suggestion before executing any of them. The first is the Sensor Reliability Weight which represents the decline in quality of a sensor over time and the second is Temporal Safety Horizon which instead of only looking at the current safety of an action, looks at the safety of the action in a short and therefore simulated, future.

However, many implementations treat oversight as an external governance layer rather than as a first-class architectural concern integrated into system design, verification, monitoring, and evolution. This creates risks related to automation bias, lack of explainability, unsafe autonomy escalation, and insufficient accountability mechanisms. This tutorial bridges software architecture, human-centered AI, and governance-aware system engineering and provides participants with a systematic approach to designing, implementing, and evaluating human oversight mechanisms across the software lifecycle.

v20_abstract: A Photovoltaic (PV) cell inside solar panels requires manufacturing through a stringent and controlled process. The PV manufacturing process faces difficulties because it contains multiple complex stages where defects can propagate without detection, which negatively impacts both efficiency and production yield. The current AI-based solutions in this domain operate through open-loop analytics, where human engagement is required to perform Root Cause Analysis (RCA) of faults, which may take multiple hours. Every minute spent on fault detection is a minute late for corrective action. Until now, industries have implemented pre-programmed fault detection with significant human intervention to diagnose faults and take corrective actions. However, with the evolution of large language models (LLMs) and reasoning models, fault detection can be made autonomous. This research develops an innovative system concept that uses LLMs-orchestrated by a Semantic Kernel as a central reasoning agent to achieve near-closed-loop control in PV manufacturing, allowing autonomous diagnosis and fault handling. This study uses synthetic data based on high-efficiency PV specifications to introduce 50 different anomalies that affect conveyor-based production stages, which would consequently result in low productivity and less efficient PV modules. The LLM agent performed a complete 50-step troubleshooting process to detect efficiency loss causes while creating detailed natural-language reports and recommending specific corrective actions for technicians or robotic systems. The system demonstrated 90% accuracy in root-cause identification through 250 experimental trials using ground-truth anomaly validation when it received a 50-step troubleshooting protocol. The research fills essential gaps in current PV manufacturing automation by tracking defects semantically throughout production stages while providing specific decisions and converting machine data into actionable language-based workflows. The proposed LLM-mediated architecture establishes a major advancement toward adaptive quality assurance systems that operate efficiently and at scale for solar panel production.
